label: GPT-6 Luna
output:
**Glenmore**

I want to tell you all properly about Glenmore, rather than have the news travel round the family in bits and pieces on the phone. Some of you have already heard, and Declan heard from Gráinne on WhatsApp before I had spoken to him. That was my doing, and I’m sorry for the way you found out. I should have told you myself.

The sale is agreed. It was agreed on 3 November, and it closes on 15 January 2027. I know that is sudden news to some of you, especially those who were expecting to talk about it when they came over in the summer. I didn’t consult Declan before I made the decision, and I regret that. But I am not willing to wait until his summer visit to say what I have decided.

Glenmore is the old Mulkerrin place near Oughterard, built in 1931 by Tom’s grandfather, Pádraig. Tom grew up there. After Tom died in March 2024, I kept going out every fortnight to open the windows, air the rooms and check the pipes. It’s a forty-minute drive each way. At first, the routine gave me something to do. I suppose I also thought that if I kept looking after the house, I was looking after something of Tom’s.

There is plenty in that house I will never forget. Tom asked me to marry him in the haggard behind it, in 1979. It was raining, of course, and the cattle were watching us. Our children learned to swim in the lake below the house. Declan, you would refuse to come out even when your lips had gone blue. I remember the house as noisy and alive: people arriving, children underfoot, wet coats drying, and all the ordinary business of a family.

Those memories are not the reason I’m selling. They are part of why it has been hard.

Last February, I slipped on the step at the back door in the frost. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could get myself up. I haven’t told anyone until now. I’m not telling you to make you feel sorry for me. I just don’t want to leave that out of the story. Since then I have been afraid of being alone at the house. I cannot keep driving out and maintaining it as though nothing has changed.

The practical side has changed too. In September I had Ó Flaithearta’s survey the roof. The slates and the back chimney need work; the quote was €38,000. There’s damp in the back bedroom, and the septic tank needs replacing if the house is to be sold to anyone. I have been trying to keep up with it all, but I can’t go on maintaining a house I’m frightened to be in by myself.

I agreed the sale with Aoife and Kevin Joyce, a young couple with two small children. Kevin is from Maam Cross. They want to live in the house, not turn it into a holiday let. That mattered to me. There were higher offers in the summer from people in Dublin, but I took the lower one on purpose. The price was fair, and I would rather see a family make a home there than have the place sit empty for most of the year.

Tom always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum. I didn’t know what to do with those words for a long time. Over the best part of two years, I’ve come to realise that I can keep Tom’s memory without keeping the house. I don’t need every room and every stone to prove that he was loved, or that our life together happened. It did. We remember it.

Some things from Glenmore are staying with the family. The dresser is going to Úna’s. I’m keeping Pádraig’s fiddle, the photographs, the Sacred Heart lamp and the gate sign. These are the things I can hold on to without trying to hold on to the whole house. The Joyces have also said that the family can come out and walk the land any time. I’m glad of that. Glenmore won’t be closed to us.

Declan, I know you were hurt when you heard from Gráinne rather than from me. You rang at two in the morning your time and said I was “selling Dad”. I was hurt and tired, and I said things back that I shouldn’t have said. I’m sorry for that, and I’m sorry you had to hear the news second-hand. I should have spoken to you properly before the sale was agreed. I didn’t, and I’m not going to pretend I handled it well.

But I am not angry with you. I understand why the house feels like more than a building, and why hearing about the sale that way made it worse. I hope you can understand that I have not made this decision because I want to leave Tom behind. I’m making it because I can’t look after the house anymore, and because I believe the Joyces will make it a home. I’m not sorry for the decision, but I am sorry for how you found out. The door is open if you want to talk.

I’d like us all to have one more family day at Glenmore before it’s cleared. We’ll meet there on Sunday, 13 December. Anyone who can come is welcome. I’ll have soup and sandwiches, and you should bring your wellies. There’s no grand plan for the day. We can walk the land, sit in the house and remember things, or just have a cup of tea together. Come if you can, and if you can’t, know you’re being thought of.

The sale closes on 15 January 2027. I wanted that date here in one place so nobody else has to hear it from someone else again. I know some of you will be sad. I am too. But sadness doesn’t mean the decision is wrong, and letting go of the house doesn’t mean letting go of each other, or of Tom.

I hope we can spend that December day together, as ourselves, and not as people arguing over a house. Bring your wellies. I’ll see you there.
